I am confused about Voat's take on this story. It would seem one of two things had to have occurred. 1) Murdock was murdered or 2) Murdock committed suicide.

1: If he was murdered, then it stands to follow that you must also believe someone else sent those tweets from his account announcing his intention to commit suicide. But if this is the case, then why would the killer implicate the police as unjustly harassing him? This makes no sense, especially if you believe the police killed him.

2: If he committed suicide and the tweets in question are actually his, it stands to reason that he was either unbalanced or mentally-ill. I'm not judging him, but a guy his age with a good job and kids doesn't just kill himself because he's had a bad run in with the police. So if he actually was suicidal, and those tweets are his, then it's pretty clear he was not reacting to this one incident. The tweets betray a person who is not thinking straight, distressed, agitated, and capable of being violent (at least towards himself). A person in this state of mind probably isn't acting very rationally and might very well be difficult if challenged by law enforcement.

In my estimation, Occam's razor suggests that #2 is the more likely of the scenarios that occurred. I'd genuinely be interested in someone attempting to make a persuasive fact-based argument to the contrary.

I can't speak for Voat's take, but can speak to why I think there are many unusual aspects to this case. Let's adhere to Occam's razor and go with your second estimation.

  1. I've never heard of Twitter closing a deceased user's account within hours of the decedent's death. Twitter, like many social media companies, is incredibly difficult to reach, at least by the general public. I'm assuming here the family asked for the account to be closed, and I'd imagine they definitely qualify as the "general public" and don't have inside contacts at Twitter. The outcome seems unusual and unexpected.

  2. If instead the police asked Twitter to close the account, that's still highly unusual as it would indicate a cover-up. I don't think this happened, but if it did it, too, is highly unusual.

  3. No one appears to have made any statements. Not the police who arrested him at least once, maybe twice. Not the EMTs the police supposedly called to triage his injuries. Not the hospital who purportedly treated his injuries and released him. Not the neighbors upon whose doors he was allegedly knocking. Given that his death may have been a suicide, it makes sense that his family isn't talking. But everyone else? At the very least some statements should have been forthcoming.

  4. Assuming he had multiple injuries outside of suicide-related injuries, there will be an investigation by the medical examiner, if for no other reason than to determine which injuries contributed to the cause of death. Anyone know if there is such an investigation?

  5. I would have expected his employer to have issued a statement after more facts were in. They were ready on Monday. Again, odd.

Thank you for your thoughtful response. Don't take what follows as an argument, but merely as points for discussion.

1: I don't know much about Twitter closing accounts either, but is there any evidence that it was closed for nefarious purposes? Murdock was an extremely well-known person in the Linux community--it seems to me that people at Twitter would be at least as aware of him as people on Voat (and in the media)...probably moreso. Seeing that his final tweets contained the word "nigger" (regardless of how he meant it), it seems very plausible that Twitter accommodated the account's removal if for no other reason than to protect his reputation. His next of kin hasn't come forward to complain or raise any concerns so that in and of itself suggests that they accept the official findings.

2: See #1 above. You are correct that it would be highly unusual, and since Twitter has a history resisting authorities attempts to gain access without warrants, I agree that it is not probable.

3: The police are not required to make a statement, and in deference to the family should not. That said, the case information is most likely public, so you can most likely get it unless a court has somehow sealed it (highly doubtful). Has any member of the press requested the arrest record and been denied? If so, what was the reason? As to the EMT, they may be bound by patient confidentiality or something like that. I certainly would not expect them to offer up unsolicited information regarding anyone's injuries. However, if Murdock was treated for injuries incident to his arrest, that information should be available from law enforcement, along with the arrest report. As for neighbors, has a reporter actually attempted to interview them and been turned away? Regardless, I still wouldn't interpret neighbors reluctance to speak to the press as suspicious. I don't like my neighbors, but if one of them were to kill themselves, I'd probably respect their family and not say anything to a reporter. Remember that Murdock was a millionaire. I assume he lived in a nice neighborhood. I'm not sure how anxious people with money are to start talking to the press about a (potentially) crazy neighbor who posted shit about "niggers" and then killed himself.

4: Not sure this is 100% accurate. There might be an autopsy that would make note of other wounds. If so, that information should become available to the public once the reports have been finalized.

5: I disagree. His employer did make a statement mourning his death. Nothing else is appropriate. No company has any business speculating about the death of one of their employees--especially one who committed suicide. Anything other than condolences are inappropriate.

Are his next of kin raising concerns about his death? If not, then any speculation of nefarious activity must then extend to his family as well. Either they are satisfied that he took his own life, or they have been threatened into silence. Barring no further information, Occam's razor suggest that they are satisfied and are (like most families that have gone through this) just wanting privacy.
